articleSummary: Researchers from the University of São Paulo and the Butantan Institute tested venoms from eight Bothrops snakes on Schistosoma mansoni, which causes visceral schistosomiasis in Latin America and Africa, assessing effects on gene expression and reproduction. Some venoms reduced locomotion, attachment, viability, and disrupted egg-laying; moojeni venom was most potent, nearly abolishing egg deposition and markedly impairing movement, while jararacuçu reduced egg laying. After incubation, male and female worms were sequenced separately, revealing a systemic collapse in males with many more genes affected than in females. Affected male genes relate to cell division and nerve signal transmission, whereas female changes pertain more to reproductive processes. The study highlights non-coding RNAs as potential therapeutic targets. Praziquantel remains the only approved drug, raising concerns about resistance. Future work aims to design synthetic molecules to target these RNAs and test them in vivo and in clinical trials, per International Journal of Molecular Sciences.

articleHeadline: Pregnant And Hepatitis : Here's What You Should Know
articleSummary: In Pune, India, hepatitis during pregnancy can be managed with testing and care, allowing most women to have healthy babies. Hepatitis A–E exist, but hepatitis B and C are most relevant during pregnancy due to potential mother-to-child transmission. If hepatitis B is detected before pregnancy, vaccinating family members, liver monitoring, and treatment can reduce preterm birth, low birth weight, and transmission. Newborn protection includes hepatitis B vaccine and hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) within 12 hours of birth, followed by complete vaccination. Hepatitis C carries a lower transmission risk and has no vaccine. Hepatitis A and E usually do not cause long-term infection in babies, though hepatitis E can be severe. Pregnant women should attend prenatal check-ups, liver function tests if advised, eat a balanced diet, avoid alcohol and unnecessary medicines, maintain hygiene and safe water, and avoid sharing needles or razors. Early screening and appropriate care support healthy outcomes.
